## People absorb what they already half know

## The analysis was ready. The decision never came.

At the start of 2026 I set out to redesign a whole value stream with agents. We picked the slice that takes a company's flagship product to its millions of customers. Many teams touch it.

We built a multi-agent system for the work. About fifteen people across those teams mapped their own part and uploaded their own documents. A central agent pulled it all into one map of how the work flows today.

On the first workshop day, most of them refined that map together. People had fun, and bit by bit they learned how it works. On the second day a smaller group redesigned the flow. We left with a plausible proposal and the analysis to decide on it.

We had chosen this topic with the senior leadership before we started. By the decision meeting, the urgency had gone. New priorities had come up, and fires were burning elsewhere. The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.

The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had. Companies, even when they go agentic, work first and foremost on the human principle.

Antti Tevanlinna

[What would have to be true for them to switch?](slides/what-would-have-to-be-true.md)

Push back where the agent's summary is wrong. *"The teammate's job wasn't vague, you just didn't see it"* / *"you pulled too much out of the skill, put the edge cases back."* The artifact: the sharpened sharing file itself, plus one line in your Module 7 next-step file naming the first move. # Lecture: Access is not absorption

One law decides whether a sharing plan works. This lecture names it and shows where it applies.

[Access is easy; absorption is scarce](slides/access-is-easy.md)

## The analysis was ready. The decision never came.

At the start of 2026 I set out to redesign a whole value stream with agents. We picked the slice that takes a company's flagship product to its millions of customers. Many teams touch it.

We built a multi-agent system for the work. About fifteen people across those teams mapped their own part and uploaded their own documents. A central agent pulled it all into one map of how the work flows today.

On the first workshop day, most of them refined that map together. People had fun, and bit by bit they learned how it works. On the second day a smaller group redesigned the flow. We left with a plausible proposal and the analysis to decide on it.

We had chosen this topic with the senior leadership before we started. By the decision meeting, the urgency had gone. New priorities had come up, and fires were burning elsewhere. The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.

The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had. Companies, even when they go agentic, work first and foremost on the human principle.

Antti Tevanlinna

## The people who mapped the work absorbed it

The fifteen people learned the system by putting their own documents into it, over two days, at their own pace. The people who had to decide received the finished analysis. They had full access to it. They had not spent any of their own weeks inside it. A sharing plan that ends when the result is delivered stops where that project stopped.

[Three parts copy, one does not](slides/three-parts-copy.md)

## Each strategy puts absorption somewhere else

When you share the context, your teammate has to absorb your curation, and that asks for the most trust. When you share a skill, they absorb one bounded capability inside an agent they already run. Shared output lands on a schedule, in a place they already look. With a shared interface, they ask in their own words when the job comes up. The right choice is the one that fits the week your teammate already has.

[What would have to be true for them to switch?](slides/what-would-have-to-be-true.md)

## One name, one small move

`module-7/monday.md` holds one person, one question about how they do the job today, and one assumption to test. The plan stays a hypothesis until that person answers. Send them a message today and ask for twenty minutes of their week. Ask the question in the file, then listen to how they do the job now.

Pick one teammate who could use what your agent produces. What would you want them to have: your folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack? Why that one?

Start a fresh session at `~/Documents/agents-101/`. The agent writes the sharing plan into `module-7/`, and `module-7/monday.md` holds the next move: one person, one question, one test.

The four sharing strategies:

1. **Share the context.** Your `memory/`, `sources/`, root `CLAUDE.md` and `style.md` travel. Teammates build their own agent on top of your curation.
2. **Share a skill.** One scoped capability, extracted as a skill file. Teammates plug it into their own agents.
3. **Share the output (push).** The agent runs on a schedule. Its output lands where the team already looks.
4. **Share an interface (pull).** The agent sits behind a bot, a mention, a form or an endpoint. Teammates ask in their own words when they need it.

## One name, one small move

`module-7/monday.md` holds one person, one question about how they do the job today, and one assumption to test. The plan stays a hypothesis until that person answers. ## Each strategy puts absorption somewhere else

When you share the context, your teammate has to absorb your curation, and that asks for the most trust. When you share a skill, they absorb one bounded capability inside an agent they already run. Shared output lands on a schedule, in a place they already look. With a shared interface, they ask in their own words when the job comes up. text:
## The analysis was ready. The decision never came.

At the start of 2026 I set out to redesign a whole value stream with agents. We picked the slice that takes a company's flagship product to its millions of customers. Many teams touch it.

We built a multi-agent system for the work. About fifteen people across those teams mapped their own part and uploaded their own documents. A central agent pulled it all into one map of how the work flows today.

On the first workshop day, most of them refined that map together. People had fun, and bit by bit they learned how it works. On the second day a smaller group redesigned the flow. We left with a plausible proposal and the analysis to decide on it.

We had chosen this topic with the senior leadership before we started. By the decision meeting, the urgency had gone. New priorities had come up, and fires were burning elsewhere. The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.

The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.

Antti Tevanlinna

## It can only use what someone wrote down

One limit worth seeing while the memory is fresh in front of you.

The agent can only work from what somebody wrote down. Most of what you know about your own company, nobody has. It sits in heads, in corridors, in the judgement of the person who has been there long enough to stop noticing they have it.

That is not a fault in the memory you built. It is why the memory you built is worth something. Every round of this moves one more piece of what you know out of your head and into something the system can read next time.

where: lectures/compounding.md · What this unlocks (Module 2)
ask: Cut whole sentences, or keep two lines that may be the motive for the step?
a:
## What this unlocks

Your memory is specific to your challenge. The question you ran through it came back with claims cited to your files, reasoning shaped by your context, a voice that isn't a generic industry take. The answer belongs to the memory you built, not to the LLM behind it. That's the point the whole training turns on: *generic AI becomes your AI when you shape the context that surrounds it.* Guardrails did this at the prompt level in Module 1. A memory does it at the knowledge level now. The mechanism is the same; only the shelf life changed.

Every module after this leans on that memory. Multi-agent systems reads from it. Security reviews it. Quality evals run against it. The flywheel in Module 8 feeds it. You didn't build a training exercise. You built the material the rest of the training runs on.
